title: Influence of Sex and Level on Marathon Pacing Strategy. Insights from the New York City Race
authors: Santos-Lozano A, Collado PS, Foster C, Lucia A, Garatachea N
population: 190,228 New York City Marathon finishers (69,316 women), 2006 to 2011, 5-km splits
findings: All runners developed a positive pace profile (slower in the second half).
Variability of speed across 5-km splits was lower in the top runners (coefficient of variation 7.8% men and 6.6% women) than in the less successful runners (coefficient of variation 8.3 to 14.4%).
Both men and women tried to hold an even pace profile, partly by avoiding an excessively fast start that might produce a pronounced fall in speed in the second half.
limitations: Retrospective results data; no weather, effort or training data; split-based variability confounds pacing with fatigue and course; the abstract gives no per-finishing-time split table.
implications: The largest road marathon pacing sample in the corpus: at every level the average finisher slowed, and less variable speed went with faster finishing. Supports a plain sentence that an even pace is the norm among faster finishers; it does not prove that an even pace causes a faster finish.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (IJSM 35:933-938, online 2014-06-02). Abstract read on Europe PMC. Crossref lists no correction, erratum or retraction notice (checked 2026-11-16).
